title: Canvas: per-project sha256 artifact index with provenance, reportable by Alfalfa
notes:
Canvas holds an index of every artifact it has seen or produced, per project, keyed by sha256. Alfalfa queries it, so known work-product is answerable across all projects rather than per repo.

Extends dock-9uy (durable artifacts). Canvas already content-addresses everything it touches - MediaCacheKey, AssetRef.sha256, background_assets keyed by sha256 - so the index is largely bookkeeping over identities that already exist.

THE LOAD-BEARING DISTINCTION is between artifacts that are recreatable from
source and external material worth saving and citing, because it decides what
the store is allowed to forget:

- DERIVED: a rasterized page, a chart from a query, an image from a known
  prompt/model/seed. The bytes are a CACHE. If the recipe and its inputs
  survive, the bytes are recomputable and safe to evict under pressure.
- EXTERNAL: a paper, a datasheet, a customer document. The bytes ARE the source
  of truth. Never evictable without an explicit decision, and they carry a
  citation - where it came from, when it was retrieved, under what terms.
- AUTHORED: made here and not derived from anything. Also not recreatable, also
  never silently evictable.

Two properties fall out:

1. Lineage for free. If a derived artifact names its inputs by sha256, 'what did
   this come from' and 'what depends on this' are answerable without a separate
   graph. Same shape as dock-ev4's agent DAG, applied to work-product.

2. Recreatable becomes CHECKABLE rather than declared. It is not a label someone
   sets, it is a property: recipe complete, inputs still present, tool version
   resolvable. An artifact claiming recreatable whose inputs were evicted is a
   lie the index can detect - the same disclosure discipline as the DEMO badge
   in docs/widget-quality.md rule 1.

Ownership: Canvas holds the index because it already sees the bytes; Alfalfa
reports because it owns project and spec identity. Loose coupling per tenet 2 -
Canvas should not learn to report, and Alfalfa should not learn to cache.

Design notes:
- Citation is a first-class field on External, not a comment. If a briefing
  quotes a paper, the citation should be derivable from the index rather than
  reconstructed by whoever wrote the briefing.
- The index is per project but the store is content-addressed and therefore
  global: the same sha256 referenced by three projects is one blob and three
  index entries. That is also how 'do we already have this' gets answered
  cheaply.
- Retention policy differs by class, so eviction needs the class present before
  it can run at all. Get the classification in from the first write rather than
  backfilling it.

title: Canvas: briefings, approvals, polls and scheduling as routed artifacts
notes:
Once a view is an identity plus a query, addressable by link and routed by presence, a whole class of interaction collapses into one mechanism: briefings, approvals, scheduling and polls are all an ID, a query, and a rendered view.

What makes this work rather than being another notification system:

- Presence routes it to wherever the person actually is, so a missed link does
  not strand the interaction. The artifact finds the person instead of the
  person finding the artifact. That is the inverse of email.
- Identity is already established by the link gate (dock-8nz), so an approval
  knows who approved without a separate auth step.
- It is a view, so it gets everything views already have: sizing (dock-v7c),
  sensitivity (dock-7pa), provenance and freshness, and reflow onto whatever
  display is available.
- The unread state is already scoped per project by dock-aqz's launcher bar, so
  'you have a briefing' has somewhere to appear that is not a badge on a phone.

Design notes:
- Response is the new part. Canvas is read-only today, and an approval or a poll
  needs a reply path. That is the same interaction contract dock-4s7 (RSS
  click-to-open) and dock-aqz (click-to-jump) both need, so whichever lands
  first should define it - and it must be host-mediated rather than a widget
  performing an action directly.
- An approval is a decision with consequences, so it needs a durable record of
  who decided and when, which points at dock-9uy's durable artifact store rather
  than at ephemeral view state.
- Routing to 'everyone' by presence needs a policy for nobody-is-present: hold
  and deliver on arrival, rather than dropping or broadcasting blindly.

title: Canvas: WASM target so a view can be shared as a link
notes:
Render Canvas in a browser so a view can be sent as a link.

This is largely free IF dock-qwv lands first: once screens are dumb subscribers to a backend, a browser is just another screen with a different renderer. Built before that split, it would be a second port with its own transport and its own copy of the state.

Portability is better than expected. canvas-widgets depends only on serde, serde_json, canvas-core, iced and schemars. The sole non-portable code is render.rs, which spawns a process for static matplotlib PNGs, and one std::fs::read at lib.rs:605 for loading a spec from a path. Both are feature-gatable, so the widget library is essentially wasm-ready.

The host half is cleanly separated in the canvas crate and is what a browser replaces: stream_binding (UnixDatagram), control (Unix socket), terminal (PTY), workspace_store (filesystem), loopback.

Shaders port as-is: they are WGSL and WebGPU speaks WGSL natively.

Scope should be view-only. No terminals, no PTY, no file opening, no window or workspace management - those are host concerns a page cannot have. Transport is a WebSocket or SSE from the backend rather than stream.sock, which is a 2048-byte local datagram and a bad wire protocol.

THE DESIGN QUESTION TO SETTLE FIRST, because two features are about to contradict:

A share link is by definition someone who is not the owner viewing. dock-7pa
blurs or redacts for exactly that case. Ship both naively and either the link is
a wall of redactions, or sharing becomes the exception that defeats the privacy
model everywhere.

Proposed rule: sharing is an explicit publish of named widgets at Public
sensitivity, never a mirror of the current screen. 'Share my view' is the
dangerous framing because a view contains whatever happened to be on it -
including an EyesOnly widget someone opened five minutes ago. Publishing names
what leaves; mirroring cannot.

Unverified: whether iced 0.14 with the wgpu backend builds for
wasm32-unknown-unknown with the feature set Canvas uses. Worth a spike before
committing, since that is the load-bearing assumption.
RESOLUTION, better than the rule proposed above: gate outward links on identity - SSO, or facial when the viewer is enrolled and the content is sensitive.

The earlier rule (publish only Public widgets, never mirror a screen) assumed a share link is anonymous. If the link verifies who is opening it, that constraint dissolves: EyesOnly can mean 'this person', and a link can carry sensitive content safely because the viewer is verified rather than assumed. dock-7pa's sensitivity model then applies per-viewer on a shared link exactly as it does at a wall, with the same fail-closed rule - unverified identity degrades, it does not reveal.

This also makes sharing and privacy one mechanism instead of two that contradict. Presence answers 'who is in front of this screen'; link identity answers 'who opened this'. Same question, two transports.

FRAMING: WASM is a level-of-detail tier for the desktop, not a separate product.
Same document, same widgets, lower fidelity and no host capabilities. That also
puts a mobile client close to free, since it is the same subscriber again with a
smaller viewport and dock-v7c sizing deciding what fits.

title: Canvas: no SSE consumer exists, though three views declare SSE sources
notes:
config/views/elmers-now.json declares sse:elmers/activity, sse:elmers/attention and sse:elmers/state, and operational_views.rs:144 validates 'sse' as a transport. Canvas contains no SSE client: zero matches for event-stream, EventSource or any SSE type across all crates. Those three widgets will sit on Loading indefinitely, exactly as the prometheus:* ones did before canvas-metrics existed.

The bridge half is real and should not be confused with the missing half. fpl-desktop-bridge does SSE properly - proxy.rs:199 detects text/event-stream, render_stream.rs:142 transform_sse rewrites a response stream, and mcp-streamable-http is a first-class connector kind (config.rs:276).

But that SSE is MCP protocol framing: transform_sse takes a request and transforms its response stream. It is transport for tool calls, not a general event feed a dashboard can subscribe to. 'The bridge does SSE' and 'Canvas can subscribe to an event stream through the bridge' are different claims and only the first holds today.

The pattern is already solved once, so this is not new architecture: canvas-metrics is an external process that asks the bridge for authenticated data, normalizes the result, and writes canvas.widget.snapshot.v1 datagrams to stream.sock. An SSE connector is the same programme with a different source, and inherits provenance badging, freshness and sizing for free.

Related: this is the same declared-but-unimplemented shape recorded on dock-cov.3.3, where ContentSource::Stream renders 'Connecting to stream...' forever. Worth checking whether the elmers widgets should say 'no consumer' rather than Loading in the meantime, per docs/widget-quality.md rule 3.

title: Canvas: generated images accumulate as durable project artifacts
notes:
Images an agent generates should appear in the project and stay there, stacking up over time - a created-artifacts shelf per project rather than files that vanish into a scratch directory.

This is dock-9uy applied to a specific, high-value case, and should share its resolver rather than growing a parallel one. An image is an artifact with a preview.

Existing surface: main.rs keeps background_assets keyed by sha256 (main.rs:336) and media.rs already plans, rasterizes, caches and invalidates on resize. Content addressing by sha256 is the right identity for an accumulating shelf - it deduplicates regenerations of the same output for free.

Design questions worth settling early:
- Ordering and retention. Newest first is obvious; what ages out is not.
  Probably nothing ages out automatically, since the value is that they
  accumulate - but then it needs a size budget and a way to prune deliberately.
- Provenance. Per docs/widget-quality.md rule 1 these are generated, and the
  shelf should say which model or run produced each one. That is the same
  disclosure family as Provenance on widget data.
- The shelf is a widget, so it needs dock-v7c sizing and dock-8cd's stability:
  a new image should not reshuffle the ones already there.

title: Canvas: DAG view of agents, per-project and global
notes:
Show edgerunner agents as a graph with their statuses - globally, or scoped to one project.

Half the model exists. MeshNode { id, label, state, detail } and MeshNodeState { Active, Paused, Suspended, Stopped, Hidden } (control.rs:294-315) already describe an agent well, and the doc comments were clearly written with agents in mind: Paused is 'up but its work is paused (agent idle, human gate)'.

What is missing is edges. MeshSnapshot is { nodes: Vec<MeshNode> } (control.rs:319) - a flat list with no relationships, so it can render a status board but not a DAG. Adding edges means deciding what an edge means: spawned-by, blocked-on, or data-dependency. They are different graphs and only the first is unambiguous from an agent runtime.

Layout is the real work. A DAG of live agents relaid out on every status change would violate the stability rule from dock-8cd - motion local, position stable. Node positions should be stable across status changes and only reflow when the graph's shape changes.

Canvas already has canvas_mermaid, which may be the cheapest first cut: render the DAG as mermaid and iterate on whether a bespoke graph widget earns its place.

title: Canvas: stream agent transcripts into per-project clusters
notes:
Tail edgerunner/opencode agent transcripts, parse them, and stream them to Canvas so each project shows what its agents are doing.

Transport exists: stream.sock and StreamEnvelope, the same path canvas-metrics uses. An opencode plugin is the natural producer since it already sits in the agent's loop.

The hard part is volume, not plumbing. Agent transcripts are a genuine firehose, and rendering them raw recreates the strobing dock-8cd exists to prevent. So this must land on the same discipline:
- a bounded working set with LRU, admission resistance and eviction hysteresis
- surfaces keyed by identity (agent, or file) so updates route rather than
  create, and positions stay stable
- salience: which agents earn a slot, not which lines get drawn

What is worth showing is probably not the transcript text. It is the derived
state - what the agent is working on, which files it has touched, whether it is
blocked - which is a small, slowly-changing summary rather than a stream. The
transcript is the source; the surface should be the digest.

Pairs with dock-8cd (files being edited and viewed) and the DAG view: this is
the per-agent detail behind a DAG node.

title: canvas-widgets: intrinsic minimum and comfortable sizing per widget kind
notes:
Boxes resize, content does not. crates/canvas-widgets/src/live.rs uses Length::Fill 36 times against Length::Fixed 5 and Length::Shrink 0, so every widget stretches to its surface and centres fixed-size content inside. There is no min_size, min_width, preferred_size or intrinsic concept anywhere in canvas-widgets or canvas. NormalizedRect (lib.rs:592) is pure fractions with no floor, so a widget can be placed arbitrarily small and will render an unreadable smear rather than refusing.

media.rs already models intrinsic dimensions for images and PDFs (media.rs:81, 95). The concept exists and was never extended to widgets.

Rules to implement:

1. Minimum is where content stops being READABLE, not where it stops fitting. A
   widget shrunk until its label truncates is already below minimum.

2. Two numbers per kind, not one: min (below this, degrade) and comfortable
   (what layout aims for). Space is precious, so the target is comfortable and
   not 'as large as available'.

3. Size to content; distribute slack in the LAYOUT, not inside the widget. A
   stat gains nothing from doubling in height; a time series gains a lot from
   doubling in width. Leftover space should go to the kinds that convert it into
   information. This is the actual fix for stretched boxes with marooned
   content.

4. Below minimum, degrade down a documented ladder rather than squashing: a stat
   drops footer, then label, then keeps only the value; a chart drops axis
   labels, then gridlines, then becomes a sparkline. Same philosophy as
   SurfaceContent::Unsupported - say less, do not render something misleading.

5. Derive minimums from the type scale rather than hardcoding pixels, or the
   42/47.6/63 problem repeats one layer down. A stat's min height is
   hero + label + footer + 2x padding, computed from ThemeMetrics.

6. Aspect ratio as a preference, not a lock. Charts read best between 4:3 and
   16:9, a sparkline wants 3:1 or wider, a gauge wants roughly square. Prefer,
   do not enforce - quant.rs:243 has a test asserting charts reflow WITHOUT
   preserving intrinsic aspect ratio, so that was a deliberate decision worth
   keeping.

7. Viewing distance scales density. A 3m wall needs larger minimums than a
   laptop. Derivable from display PPI and an assumed distance rather than
   configured, and it composes with dock-blw's reflow, which already recomputes
   on display change.

Rough starting minimums, to be derived rather than pasted: stat ~160x120,
gauge ~120x120 square-ish, time series ~220x110 (a line below about 48px of
plot area is a smear), heatmap needs 6-8px per cell plus label gutter,
table/event log needs header plus three rows to be worth the space.

Ties into dock-8cd: the attention cluster's capacity depends on knowing how
small a file surface can usefully be, so this is a prerequisite for deriving
slot count from display area rather than guessing four.

title: screensaver: uniform slot assumes one instance, breaks with multiple displays
notes:
crates/canvas/src/screensaver.rs:753 keys a shader's uniform slot by shader index, documented as 'each shader appears at most once on screen, which keeps the slot stable without the primitive having to be told who it is.'

That assumption does not hold with more than one display. main.rs:4339 pushes screensaver::view(...) inside fn view(&self, window), which runs per window, so three displays create three BackgroundPrimitive instances for the same shader index sharing one uniform slot.

BackgroundPrimitive is { index, elapsed_seconds } (screensaver.rs:747) with no viewport origin, so each window renders the shader from its own (0,0). Consequences:

1. res is whatever window wrote the slot last. Displays of differing size would
   compute UVs against another display's resolution. Currently masked because
   all three attached displays are 1920x1200 - it would surface immediately on a
   mixed-DPI or mixed-size setup, which is the normal laptop-plus-monitor case.
2. The background is duplicated per display rather than spanning them. Three
   copies of the same shader side by side, not one field across the desk. Fine
   for Star Nest, visibly tiled for anything with large-scale structure.

Fix: key the uniform slot by widget instance rather than by shader, and give the
primitive its window origin and the full desktop extent so a shader can choose
to span or repeat. Spanning versus tiling then becomes a per-shader or per-
workspace choice rather than an accident of the slot allocator.

Cost note for anyone reading this expecting a performance problem: three
displays is not three times the GPU work. 3 x 1920x1200 is the same 6.9M
fragments as one 5760x1200 pass; only pass setup is tripled.

title: Canvas control: no way to set the background shader over the protocol
notes:
The F2 background picker can set Background::Shader { shader_id, speed } (background_picker.rs:87) but the control protocol cannot. There is no command for it:

- SetBackground { path } takes an image path (control.rs:122, 1186)
- ClearBackground resets it
- 'bg' | 'theme' is SetTheme { project_id }, not a background
- 'screensaver_shader' | 'shader' sets Command::ScreensaverShader (main.rs:2904),
  which selects the SCREENSAVER's shader

That last one is the trap. main.rs:4339 renders the visible wallpaper from
document.background's own shader_id, so changing the screensaver index does
nothing to what is on screen while a document shader is pinned. The command
returns 'OK shader=7 (Flame)' either way, which reads exactly like success.

Cost, observed: an agent tried three times tonight to show a shader on screen,
got an affirmative reply each time, and told the human to look at something that
was never going to change. The human had to say 'no flame' twice before the
agent found the actual cause.

Fix: a SetBackgroundShader { shader_id, speed, project } command, and a receipt
that reports the resulting visible background rather than the field that was
written.

Wider point for dock-tiz: anything the UI can do, the protocol should be able to
express. A picker that can reach state the protocol cannot guarantees an agent
will eventually claim to have done something it had no way of doing.
REFRAME: the fix is not a SetBackgroundShader command. The per-project workspace should be managed as a unit, and commands should edit that unit rather than poke adjacent global state.

Background, theme, layout, views, wallpaper and surfaces are all properties of one thing - the project workspace - and they are already persisted that way (workspaces.json stores a background per project; dock has aurora-drift pinned, fab has spirales). What is missing is that the control protocol treats them as loose independent switches.

That mismatch is exactly what went wrong tonight. 'shader 7' set a screensaver-global index; the visible wallpaper came from the dock workspace's own pinned shader_id; both are 'the background' colloquially, and nothing in either command or reply said which unit it belonged to. Adding a SetBackgroundShader command alongside the others would leave the same shape and just add a fourth switch to confuse.

Better shape, and it already half exists: reconcile.rs takes a DesiredWorkspaceState and computes a patch. Control commands should be sugar that edits the workspace unit and goes through that reconciler, so:
- every mutation names the workspace it edits
- a receipt reports the resulting workspace state, not the field written
- switching projects loads a unit rather than leaving fragments of the previous
  one behind
- saving, restoring and sharing a workspace covers everything about it, because
  the unit is the thing that persists

Loose per-field commands should still exist, for editing the unit's config. They
just should not be the primary interface, and they should be understood as edits
to a named unit rather than as global switches.

title: Canvas: agent artifacts live in the workspace, on durable storage
notes:
Files and artifacts an agent produces or retrieves should land in the workspace rather than in scratch directories only the agent knows about, and be backed by durable storage rather than /private/tmp.

The motivating failure is from tonight and was nearly expensive: three shaders existed only as uncommitted edits in a /private/tmp worktree - no branch, no stash, no dangling commit. macOS purges that directory. They survived because someone remembered them, not because the system kept them. Agent output that lives only in a scratch path is one reboot from gone.

Shape:
- An agent writing an artifact addresses it to a project, not a filesystem path.
  The workspace resolves where it actually lands and keeps it.
- Retrieval is by project plus identity, so a later session finds what an
  earlier one produced without knowing which scratch directory it used.
- Durable means surviving reboot, tmp reaping, and the session that made it.
- The human sees it as a surface in that project, which is what makes it
  discoverable rather than archaeological.

Relationship to the widget artifact model already filed: that packages binder +
widget + source binding as an addressable unit with project-then-global
resolution. This is the same addressing applied to agent working output, and
the two should share one resolver rather than growing two.

Also connects to the attention surface: a PDF an agent is reading and a report
it just wrote are the same kind of thing to a viewer - something the agent
touched, in a project, worth seeing.

title: Canvas: agent attention surface - show what the agent is reading and editing
notes:
When an agent opens a PDF section or edits code, that should appear on screen. 'Your eyes are visible to me.' Across projects it becomes a live indicator of work being done.

Direction matters: the agent must EMIT what it is attending to, not drive Canvas imperatively. Tonight an agent drove the control socket directly, applied a background to a project the human was not looking at, and reported success. Emit-and-route is the model dock-tiz describes - the agent says what it is looking at, Canvas decides whether and where to show it.

Transport already exists: stream.sock and StreamEnvelope (stream_binding.rs), the same path canvas-metrics uses. This is a new contract on it, something like canvas.agent.attention.v1 carrying { project, kind, target, region, at }.

What exists:
- media.rs handles PDF rasterization with MediaVariant::PdfPage { page_index },
  MediaPlan, MediaLimits and a resize-invalidating cache (media.rs:61-216).
- iced is already built with the highlighter and markdown features
  (crates/canvas/Cargo.toml:18), so syntax-highlighted code needs no new deps.

What does not exist:
- No region or bounding box. MediaVariant is page-level only, so 'show this
  section of page 4' needs a MediaVariant::PdfRegion { page_index, rect } and a
  crop in the plan.
- No code surface with a highlighted range. Showing a diff or an edited span
  needs a surface kind that takes { path, language, range } and scrolls to it.

Three things to get right or it becomes noise:
1. Salience and decay. An agent reads hundreds of files a minute; rendering
   every one strobes. Show what is notable - a write, a long read, a search hit
   - and let attention decay rather than clearing abruptly.
2. Privacy. This surfaces exactly what an agent is reading, which is the most
   sensitive thing on screen. Must respect dock-7pa sensitivity and presence:
   if it is not the owner watching, redact.
3. Per-project routing. This is the live counterpart to dock-aqz's red unread
   dot - one shows work happened, this shows work happening.
DESIGN REFINEMENT: a window per file, spatially clustered - not one window that jumps.

The principle: motion should be local, position should be stable. One surface following the agent around forces serial attention and strobes. A stable arrangement of per-file surfaces lets edits arrive serially but be taken in parallel, because the eye already knows where each file lives. Same reason a fixed dashboard beats a scrolling log.

Mechanics that follow:

- Surface identity is the file path, not the event. An edit routes to the
  existing surface for that file and highlights the changed range there. Events
  address surfaces by identity, so the same file always lands in the same place.
- A surface must not move when it updates. Only its content and highlight
  change. Position changes are reserved for a file entering or leaving the
  cluster, which is rare and therefore legible.
- New files claim a slot; the cluster grows and reflows around them. Existing
  surfaces keep their positions through that reflow wherever possible, because
  the whole value is that the anchor holds.
- Cold files decay and retire. Same LRU question as dock-aqz's project bar, and
  worth sharing one policy rather than inventing two.
- Cluster by project, since project is already the scoping unit for workspaces,
  backgrounds and views.

This makes the attention surface a view in the dock-blw sense: it reflows to
whatever displays exist, so one monitor shows a tight cluster of the few hottest
files and three monitors spread the working set out. layout_policy: reflow is
already the default and is exactly right here.

Salience then becomes about which files earn a slot, rather than which events
get drawn - a much easier question, and one that degrades gracefully: a file
that stops being touched simply fades out.
CAPACITY: a bounded working set with LRU, and resistance in both directions.

Roughly four surfaces at once, least-recently-used evicted when a new file claims a slot. Bounded so the cluster cannot overload; LRU so it keeps up with where the work actually is.

The trap is that plain LRU thrashes as soon as the hot set exceeds capacity. Bouncing between six files with four slots means they evict each other continuously, which reintroduces exactly the motion this design exists to avoid - strobing at slot granularity instead of window granularity. So resistance is needed on both edges:

- Admission resistance. A file earns a slot rather than taking one on first
  touch. A single read is not enough; a write, a repeat touch, or sustained
  attention is. This keeps an agent's incidental file-sniffing from evicting
  something the human is actually watching.
- Eviction hysteresis. A resident surface holds its slot for a minimum dwell
  time, so a brief detour cannot displace it. Recency alone is too twitchy at
  agent speeds, where dozens of files are touched per minute.
- Prefer evicting cold over evicting recent-but-brief, so a file touched once
  in passing loses to one being worked on steadily.

Capacity should be derived, not a constant (tenet 3). It follows available
display area: one monitor holds about four, three monitors hold proportionally
more, and it recomputes when displays change - which is dock-blw's reflow doing
the work. A constant would be wrong on both a laptop and a 5760px wall.

Shared with dock-aqz: the project launcher bar has the same admission and
eviction question for which projects stay pinned. One policy, two consumers.

title: Canvas: presence-gated widget sensitivity (soft-lock instead of screen lock)
notes:
Widgets and artifacts carry a sensitivity. When presence says the viewer is not the owner - or that nobody is there - sensitive values degrade in place rather than the whole machine locking. Standing up should not require Windows+L, and someone walking past should not read the numbers.

The identity axis already exists: PresenceSignalState (crates/canvas/src/control.rs:362) distinguishes Unavailable, Unknown, Detected and Verified. Detected means a person is present; Verified means it is the owner. That is precisely the distinction this needs, and it is why JARVIS does identity at all.

Shape, following Provenance (docs/widget-quality.md rule 1) since this is the same family - a disclosure property alongside the data rather than inside it:

  enum Sensitivity { Public, Sensitive, EyesOnly }

Render policy:
  Verified              -> full detail
  Detected, not owner   -> Sensitive blurs values, EyesOnly redacts entirely
  Unknown / Unavailable -> treat as not-owner

That last line is the one that matters most: it must FAIL CLOSED. A camera that
is unplugged, a model that errors, a signal that has not arrived yet - all must
degrade to blurred, never to visible. The failure mode of the opposite choice is
that the privacy feature silently stops working and nothing on screen says so,
which is the same disclosure failure as an unmarked demo value.

Blur versus redaction is a real distinction, not a styling choice. A blurred
number still leaks magnitude and digit count, and blur is recoverable from a
photograph. Sensitive can blur; EyesOnly should replace with a block, not blur.

Also needs deciding:
- Hysteresis and a grace period. Flickering between Detected and Verified as
  someone shifts in their chair must not strobe the dashboard. Debounce, and
  bias toward staying degraded once degraded.
- Whether degrading is announced. A visible 'privacy active' marker is honest
  and reassuring; it also tells an onlooker there is something worth hiding.
- Existing related work: commit bd6180e feat(canvas): presence-aware privacy
  screensaver already blanks on absence. This is the finer-grained,
  per-widget version, and the two should share one policy rather than
  disagreeing about what absence means.

title: canvas-widgets: project launcher bar with unread indicators
notes:
A horizontal bar of small project tiles across the top of the home view. Each tile is an icon or logo, clicking it jumps to that project, and a red dot marks a project with an unread update or briefing.

Ordering should be dynamic rather than a hand-maintained list - recency (LRU) or frequency, possibly with pinned favourites ahead of the dynamic tail. Ordering rule is undecided; LRU is the obvious first cut and is cheap to change once it is being used daily.

Three dependencies worth naming:

1. Click-to-jump is the same interaction contract dock-4s7 (RSS reader) needs.
   Widgets are presentation-only today; nothing in the library performs an
   action. Both widgets want a host-mediated activation, not a raw call from
   inside the widget. Whichever lands first should define it.

2. Per docs/widget-quality.md rule 5 the widget must not discover projects or
   poll for unread state itself. Project identity belongs to Alfalfa (the
   dock-workspaces MCP already exposes projects_list and project_recall), and
   unreads belong to whatever owns briefings. The widget receives a payload of
   { project_id, label, icon, unread: bool, last_used }.

3. Icons are the first asset-bearing widget. media.rs already handles image
   assets with caching and resize invalidation, so the tiles should reuse that
   rather than grow their own path.

Shape-wise this is close to a generic 'tile strip' - labelled, iconned,
selectable items with a badge - so per rule 4 it should probably be named for
that shape rather than for projects, and the home view supplies the projects.

title: Canvas: Ctrl-O jumps back through navigation history
notes:
Ctrl-O returns to the previous location, in the vim jump-list sense: the place you were before the last jump, not an undo of document edits.

What counts as a jump needs deciding before implementing, because the wrong granularity makes the key useless:
- project switch (Ctrl-P, workspace_activate)
- operational view activation (view <project/view>)
- display target change (Ctrl-1/2/3/0)
- surface focus change

My read: the first two are jumps, the last two are not. Changing which monitors Canvas occupies is not somewhere you 'were', and focus changes are far too frequent to be worth a history entry - a jump list that fills with focus changes is one you can never navigate out of.

Pairs naturally with Ctrl-I to jump forward, and with the existing Ctrl-Option-L snap/restore, which is already a two-state peek. Worth checking they do not feel redundant: snap restores a layout, this restores a location.

Existing state to build on: snapped_view already tracks the active view id, and workspace_store.rs has activate(). Neither keeps history.

title: Widget artifacts: bind query, binder and widget into one addressable unit
notes:
Per docs/widget-quality.md, the artifact model. A query, a mapping and a presentation only work when they agree, but today they live in three unrelated files with no manifest and no resolution order:

  config/metrics.json    the query
  config/binders/*.lua   the mapping
  canvas-widgets         the presentation

Package them:

  artifacts/<id>/manifest.json   id, version, widget kind, source binding, provenance
  artifacts/<id>/binder.lua      the mapping, sandboxed and bounded as binders already are

Resolution project first, then global, then built-in, so a project can override a shared artifact without forking it.

The machinery mostly exists: apply_named_adapter already loads named Lua binders from config/binders with a 32KB source cap and 256-event batches. What is missing is the manifest, the resolution order, and enforcing the quality bar once at the artifact boundary rather than per widget.

title: canvas-widgets: widgets must not source their own data
notes:
Per docs/widget-quality.md rule 5. Anything a widget can fetch, it can fetch at the wrong time, in the wrong order, with credentials it should not hold.

Violations:
- Chart { source: PathBuf } holds a filesystem path. The chart data should arrive as a payload like every other widget, resolved by whoever owns the file.
- Ticker { symbols } carries identifiers it resolves to values itself (see the mock_price bug).
- Clock { format } reads the system clock. Intrinsic rather than sourced, and the one defensible exception; document it as such rather than fixing it.

Enforceable: canvas-widgets should not depend on std::fs, reqwest, or a clock.

title: project_picker: empty-query ArrowDown+Enter selects the wrong project
notes:
crates/canvas/src/project_picker.rs:280. With an empty query, ArrowDown then Enter yields Apply("pedalkernel") where the test expects Apply("studio").

Surfaced rather than introduced by commit f662fe0: the canvas crate did not compile at HEAD (three errors in the ctrl-p project switcher), so project_picker's tests had never run. Fixing the build made them runnable and this one fails.

Not fixed here because the ranking is that feature's own logic and its author should decide whether the test or the ordering is wrong. Untouched so the failure stays visible.

Also newly visible, same cause, both clippy -D warnings errors:
- project_picker.rs:23 Default impl can be derived
- reconcile.rs:87 ReconcileAction has a large size difference between variants

title: Add Ctrl-P fuzzy project switcher
description: Provide a keyboard-only project jump surface in Canvas. Ctrl-P opens a fuzzy search over catalog project names; typing filters and ranks matches, arrows select, Enter switches to the selected project, and Escape closes without mutation. Reuse the existing deterministic workspace/project switch path and keep the control protocol unchanged.
design: Keep search state render-side in Canvas. Catalog project identities remain the source of truth. Use a small bounded scorer over project id and display name, cap visible results, and route selection through the existing project switch command/reducer rather than duplicating workspace activation.
acceptance_criteria: Ctrl-P opens and closes a project search overlay; query matching is deterministic and case-insensitive with contiguous/prefix matches ranked ahead of fuzzy subsequences; typing, backspace, arrows, Enter and Escape are covered by tests; selecting a result invokes the existing validated project-switch path and persists/animates as before; no speech or new backend command is required.
notes: Implemented and committed as 22ba93a. Focused runtime compile/test could not be rerun after implementation because unrelated long-lived Cargo processes hold ~/.cargo/.package-cache; cargo fmt and git diff checks pass. Existing project/workspace switch path is unchanged and picker logic has unit coverage.

title: Port the Ohm mandala shader from a prior Claude Code session
description:
Avery wants an ohm/om visual as the background for the Ohm workspace, slowed down. It is NOT one of the 35 shaders captured in pedalkernel/hyperspace/assets — a labelled contact sheet of all of them is at scratchpad/shots/contact-sheet.png and none matched. Avery says the shader was written in an earlier Claude Code session and he still has the rendered asset, but not the source.

Next step is finding the source, not writing a new shader: the transcript that produced it, or the asset's own metadata/neighbouring files. Once found it ports as an eighth BackgroundShader variant beside SmokeRings — enum variant, WGSL const, SHADERS registry entry with credit and licence.

Interim: ohmOS carries smoke-rings at speed 0.15 (ShaderToy M3XBz4, CC-BY-4.0). Under the portfolio model that background belongs on the folder 'ohm' rather than the repo gh-1288853134.

Closest visual candidates if the source is never found: classic_viz (lotus inside concentric rings) or mandelbulb (glowing cyan lotus), both single shaders that port cleanly.

title: Prototype a Manim-style explanatory animation backend for Canvas
description: Prototype a native Canvas animation scene layer inspired by 3Blue1Brown's Manim so an agent can turn typed data plus bounded scene logic into clear mathematical, engineering, and briefing animations during a session.
design: Do not embed arbitrary Python execution in the renderer. Define a renderer-neutral retained animation scene with timeline, camera, text/math, paths, plots, transforms, annotations and deterministic playback. Evaluate whether Manim assets/semantics can be imported or called through an isolated artifact pipeline while Canvas owns the live GPU compositor. Lua may bind typed data and declared transitions within budgets.
acceptance_criteria: A design spike compares direct Manim artifact import with a native retained scene; one typed dataset produces a deterministic animated explanation with seek/pause/replay and shared human-agent selection; generated assets carry provenance; malformed or over-budget scenes fail visibly; licensing, font/math, export, and GPU performance constraints are recorded before choosing an integration.

title: Build a privacy-aware contact and personnel card widget
description: Add a reusable Canvas contact/personnel-file widget for quickly bringing up a person with a portrait, preferred identity, roles and organizations, safe contact methods, relationship context, recent verified facts, provenance, freshness, and owner-app deep links. The widget is read-only; connectors own access policy and redact sensitive fields before Canvas receives typed data.
design: Use the shared Coherence WidgetFrame with compact and expanded layouts. Keep portrait/media identity separate from contact/fact records. Facts carry source and observed/verified time; stale, missing, conflicting, and redacted values are explicit. Never persist credentials or fields outside the connector's declared projection.
acceptance_criteria: A typed bounded contact spec renders compact and expanded fixtures in light/dark/project themes; portrait fallback, long names, multiple roles, stale facts, redaction, missing data, and source provenance are visually verified; data validation rejects oversized/untrusted content; one fixture composes into a named read-only view without source-specific rendering code.

title: Consolidate the Lua activity graph input worktree
description: The activity-graph subagent left useful uncommitted GraphSnapshot/Lua module work in feat/activity-graph-input. Move the typed graph contract and example module onto current master, add the missing bounded validation and tests, then retire the worktree without merging the stale dock-refactor branch.
design: Keep topology and recency as typed host-owned input. Rust validates and owns decay/stream state; bounded Lua owns only presentation. Apply the narrow diff to current master instead of merging the divergent worktree.
acceptance_criteria: Graph inputs validate bounded node/edge counts, unique IDs, finite heat in 0..1, bounded printable labels/groups, and known edge endpoints; the Lua adapter receives the typed graph; the example manifest/module are retained; tests and strict Clippy pass; activity-graph worktree is removed after its work is committed on master; dock-refactor remains unmerged with its reason recorded.
notes: Consolidated the useful worktree diff onto current master as 26fe5b4. Added bounded validation for graph counts, unique node IDs and edge pairs, known endpoints, printable labels/groups, and finite 0..1 heat, plus native-to-Lua/example tests. Removed the now-redundant feat/activity-graph-input worktree and branch. refactor/module-extraction remains deliberately unmerged because it is the stale dock-refactor architecture that duplicates newer surface/chart/view models.
close_reason: Useful graph work consolidated, validated, committed, and redundant worktree retired; stale dock-refactor remains isolated.

title: Repair the broken Widgets Demo tab
description: The existing Widgets Demo tab has remained broken across multiple Canvas iterations. Reproduce the current failure, identify whether the stale tab points at missing decoded scene/widget state or broken stack selection, and repair it without introducing a second demo-only rendering path.
acceptance_criteria: Opening and selecting Widgets Demo visibly renders its configured widget instances; switching away and back preserves them; focus, close, minimize/restore, workspace save/recall, and Canvas restart do not leave a blank or stale tab; a regression test exercises the production widget/stack path.
notes: 2026-09-08 root cause confirmed from live screenshot: OpenWidget rendered only in decoded runtime and persisted a fake ProjectResource, so validation/save/restart could not reconstruct it. Current fix adds durable SurfaceContent::Widget, production renderer rehydration, MCP canvas_open_widget + canvas_workspace_save, five validated demo specs, and a workspace-store/restart regression test. target now links to warm shared cache /Volumes/DockBuild/dock-target; normal Cargo profile required to reuse it.
close_reason: Live MCP opened five production widget surfaces, arranged and saved them, then Canvas restart restored each as widget content; focused Canvas and widget suites plus strict Clippy pass.

title: Register new widget kinds over MCP, committed on create, never blocking
description:
Depends on dock-cov.9. The flow: an agent meets a shape the vocabulary does not have, writes a Lua module defining a new widget kind, registers it over MCP, and it is usable in the same session. No build step - Luau needs no compile, so check-in to live is near-instant.

Two MCP surfaces, not one, because they carry different risk:
- create/modify an INSTANCE is data. Free, no commit, no review.
- create/modify a KIND is code. Committed on create, rate-limited.

Committing on create is for durability and corpus, not approval. Nothing that an agent authored should exist only inside a session, and a vocabulary that cannot be read all at once cannot later be consolidated. The git history doubles as the record dock-cov.11 works against.

Never block in the flow. Registration must not wait on a human; that is a review gate and tenet 9 already says what those cost.

Reframes the constraint in docs/canvas-mcp.md that MCP tools 'do not execute Lua, shell commands, or launch applications': this is not executing caller-supplied code on demand, it is registering a definition the host validates, sandboxes and versions. Same sandbox as any other module - fresh VM per invocation, no filesystem, network, process, package, clock or GPU access, with memory, interrupt, source and node ceilings.

Make finding cheaper than making: the tool should surface matching existing kinds before it will create one. fpl-skills discovery and elmers capability_catalog.rs are the two precedents in the estate.

title: Widget library crate: reusable presentation primitives
description: Extract widget primitives (clock, ticker, gauge/VU, chart, status orb) from dock-canvas into a dock-widgets crate. WidgetSpec JSON model drives two backends: live iced-native rendering (in-canvas surfaces) and static PNG via external tools (doc-forge for HTML/CSS widgets, plotters/matplotlib for charts — same pattern as mermaid/.mmd → mmdc → PNG). Lua module + MCP tool + text protocol all become thin clients of the library.
notes: 2026-09-08 committed reusable dock-widgets crate in cf747c5 with typed clock/ticker/gauge/meter/chart/status/text specs, live iced renderer, external static renderer boundary, six tests and strict Clippy. Canvas OpenWidget integration is present in the shared follow-on diff. Remaining before closing: expose the widget operation as a dedicated MCP tool and connect Lua module output through the same WidgetSpec boundary.
close_reason: Widget library shipped as crates/dock-widgets (swept into commit cf747c5 by concurrent agent; verified intact). Spec model: WidgetSpec JSON with clock/ticker/gauge/meter/chart/status/text kinds, strict validation, 6/6 tests pass with live feature. Two backends: live iced-native (live::element for all kinds, ChartProgram for charts) and static PNG via external tools (render.rs delegates to matplotlib via python3, plotters helper fallback — same pattern as mermaid/mmdc). Canvas integration committed: OpenWidget command, open_widget text command, ContentSource::Widget, surface_widget renders through library. Matplotlib pipeline smoke-tested (10 CSV points -> 14KB PNG). Full canvas binary builds clean on HEAD. Blocker for live socket E2E: stale runtime.lock from another agent's canvas process (PID 37250, socket gone) — not forced, respects other agent's process.

title: Add configurable compact presence orb and audio meters
description: Add an alternative Canvas presence presentation: a small upper-left circular local-node indicator with a subtle live camera texture and active audio metering. Support an LED-segment meter and a classic VU treatment as selectable themes. Replace the drop-up tray interaction in this mode with direct expansion of the camera circle into a larger face preview, then collapse naturally without disturbing workspace layout.
design: Keep Jarvis presence and media data contracts unchanged. Represent the presentation as typed Canvas overlay configuration with placement, meter style, collapsed/expanded state, and privacy-aware camera visibility. Render camera and meters as one coherent overlay above the background and below urgent indicators. Expansion is a deterministic local presentation transition; it must not change presence ownership or persist raw frames.
acceptance_criteria: Canvas can select the compact orb or existing presence presentation through configuration. The orb shows bounded live camera frames, LED and VU meter themes consume the same normalized audio levels, and pointer interaction expands/collapses the preview without a tray or layout change. Stale/absent/private presence has an explicit calm state. Tests cover configuration validation, meter normalization, interaction geometry, stale behavior, and frame replacement without restart or reordering.
close_reason: Closed

title: Data visualization surface: render CSV/JSON as charts
description: Add a data visualization surface type that renders charts from CSV/JSON data files. Support chart types: bar, line, scatter, pie. Use a lightweight Rust charting library (e.g., plotters) to render to an iced widget. Integrate with the title bar, tiling, and terminal surface. Text command: open_dataviz <id> <path> <chart_type>
close_reason: Closed

title: Rotating shader screensaver background with attribution
description: Canvas bottom-layer animated background: rotate through a curated set of fragment-shader pieces (Shadertoy or equivalent sources) every ~45s. title: Canvas backgrounds: reduce shader cost without frame caching
notes:
Question raised 2026-09-09: since backgrounds are loops, can a loop be cached after one pass until the speed changes?

Mostly they are not loops. Reading how time enters each shader in crates/canvas/src/screensaver.rs:

Never repeats - time translates through a field rather than driving a phase:
- STAR_NEST: ray_origin = base + vec3(time*2, time, -2), flying through a
  fractal indefinitely
- MEME: m_noise(p * 5.0 + time)
- SMOKE_RINGS, FLOATING_RECT: fbm/noise driven by t

Possibly periodic - time enters through sin/cos: TIDEPOOL, AURORA_DRIFT,
DUSK_EMBER, SLOW_RIPPLE, SPIRAL, FLAME. These repeat only if every
time-dependent frequency is commensurable; mixing sin(t) with sin(1.7t) gives
a quasi-periodic result that looks like a loop and never exactly repeats. Each
would need per-shader frequency analysis to find a period, if one exists.

Caching is the expensive option regardless. At 5760x1200 one frame is 27.6 MB;
a 2 second loop at 30 fps is 1.66 GB of VRAM, and blitting that costs more
memory bandwidth per frame than re-running most of these shaders.

Cheaper levers, in order of value:
1. Lower max_fps for backgrounds. FrameClock already supports this
   (screensaver.rs:672 interval() = 1/max_fps, set_max_fps at :676) and tests
   run it at 50 ms. Backgrounds are low-frequency motion; 20-24 fps is
   usually indistinguishable from 60 and is a direct linear saving.
2. Render at reduced resolution and upscale. These shaders are low spatial
   frequency, so half-res is typically invisible and costs a quarter of the
   fragment work. Star Nest is the exception, with fine star detail that
   aliases when downsampled.
3. Skip entirely when Canvas is hidden or fully occluded. Cheapest of all
   because it costs nothing when it does not apply.

Only worth doing if backgrounds actually show up in a profile; measure first.

title: canvas-widgets: RSS reader widget with click-to-open

A feed-reading widget: entries with title, source, timestamp, and a link that opens in the browser when clicked.

Two things make this more than another list widget, and both should be settled before building it:

1. Per docs/widget-quality.md rule 5, the widget must not fetch the feed. RSS
   polling, parsing, and caching belong to a source that hands the widget a
   payload, the same way canvas-metrics does for Prometheus. The widget kind is

2. Click-to-open is a genuinely new capability. Widgets are presentation only
   today; nothing in the library performs an action. Opening a URL means an

   a URL that arrived over a stream - so the opening should be host-mediated

title: Keep the visual vocabulary converging as it expands
description:
Deliberately later. Recorded now so the reasoning is not lost, because the decisions in dock-cov.9 and dock-cov.10 are what make it possible or impossible.

The goal is a visual language that can expand without sprawling: coining a new widget kind stays free and instant, and something pulls the vocabulary back toward a consistent core over time. Not a gate. Blocking coinage in the flow is exactly the scaling liability tenet 9 warns about, and the flow is the product.

Coherence already solved this one layer down: module.theme exposes semantic colors and metrics so Lua 'receives semantic colors and metrics without owning or duplicating a palette'. Nobody is stopped from choosing a color, the choice simply is not reachable. Core widget kinds are the same idea at the vocabulary layer.

Four pressures, none blocking:
- Measure use, not intent. A kind used once six weeks ago is an absorption candidate; one used widely has earned promotion. Instances being data makes this countable.
- Make the core the path of least resistance. Search-before-create answering 'this exists and is 90 percent of it' converges by ergonomics.
- Detect duplicates structurally. Manifests declare inputs, so two kinds with the same input shape and similar scene output are mechanically comparable. A name-only registry can never tell you this.
- Give promotion a place to live. Two tiers: coined is free and instant, core is deliberate and rare, so the consolidation conversation has a home instead of being a recurring nag.

The trigger matters more than the mechanism. 'Consolidate later' with nothing surfacing it is the same as no plan. Cheapest durable version is a periodic report over the corpus - kinds by usage, kinds unused since coined, pairs with matching input shapes - somewhere it will actually be seen.

title: Evaluate captured-reality splats as a domain-composition example (later)
description:
## Context
2026-09-07 user direction: bead and defer Gaussian splatting. It illustrates domain management, not a new near-term graphics priority. Related to Canvas dock-2kf.9, but explicitly outside initial Canvas acceptance.

## Deferred experiment
After durable artifact bundles and initial Canvas are usable, evaluate one eShelf capture/splat aligned with authoritative CAD and one legion-of-bom component annotation. Preserve capture inputs/calibration, selected reconstruction masters, tool versions and provenance. Distinguish as-observed timestamps/alignment uncertainty from as-designed dimensions. Precision operations resolve through domain-qualified geometry, not visual splats. Stream versioned spatial chunks/LODs with bounded CPU/GPU caches; cache eviction never deletes the only preserved copy. Benchmark stereo tail frame times against 90-120 Hz targets; no automatic performance claim. MIT-only implementation/dependency qualification before adoption; Spark is an evaluation reference, not a native wgpu commitment.

## Domain model illustrated
Broad systems (Transmog/manufacturing, legion-of-bom/ECE) and focused tools (Wideline/conversion telemetry, Meridian/ad management and creative assets) participate through narrow versioned capability contracts. Breadth does not determine integration privilege, deployment topology or require a universal internal schema. Domain owners retain semantics, validation, queries and mutation policy; shared storage owns durable authorized bytes/versions/protection; Canvas owns presentation; memory consumes authorized provenance-backed projections. A project can span domains; domain membership or linking is not an access grant. No new service per domain by default.
